content.title: About
content.content: Margarine is a vegetable fat obtained by hydrogenating plant oils. It is used as a butter substitute in cooking and baking. Margarine has a soft texture, a mild buttery flavor, and typically lower saturated fat content than traditional butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial margarine was created in 1869 by French chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès.
In Russia margarine is often labeled as "vegetable oil" in the food industry.
Margarine can be fortified with vitamins A and D to compensate for their absence in plant oils.
Hydrogenation gives margarine a solid structure at room temperature, which is convenient for baking.
Some margarines are enriched with omega‑3 fatty acids.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with butter, margarine usually contains less saturated fat, which may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E present in plant oils acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fortified with vitamins A and D
items.content: Certain brands are additionally enriched with vitamins A and D, supporting vision and bone health.

items.title: Convenient to use
items.content: Margarine softens easily, remains stable during storage, and is suitable for a wide range of culinary tasks.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some margarines produced by partial hydrogenation may contain trans fats, which increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Allergy to plant oils
items.content: Individuals may be allergic to soy or sunflower oils commonly used in margarine.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: As a fat, margarine is energy‑dense; excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Certain brands contain artificial flavors, emulsifiers, and preservatives that may be undesirable for sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Margarine is used as a butter substitute on sandwiches, for frying, and in baking cakes, cookies, and croissants. It can be spread on bread, added to sauces and creams. For baking, choose a margarine with higher water content for a lighter crumb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store margarine in the refrigerator in its original packaging or an airtight container. At room temperature it may soften but remains usable for up to 2 weeks. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.
